newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - EMU urgency fails to convince all banks.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - EMU urgency fails to convince all banks.

text.p: Banks stand to make -- or lose -- the most from European economic and monetary union (EMU), but there is mounting concern many will find themselves unprepared for the biggest event to hit financial markets this century.
It would be easy to assume that banking groups are busily installing trading teams and defining internal strategies for "E-day" -- the deadline for the single European currency.

Yet research by Reuters into at least 15 major banks shows operational strategies vary from the super-organised to those who have only just begun to assess the implications of EMU, which is only about two years away.

At one end of the spectrum, there is talk of relocating dealers out of London to centres such as Frankfurt and Paris, EMU booklets are being produced, training is on the agenda, and working groups and taskforces are all the rage.
At the other end, a "wait and see" attitude prevails and preparations are still in their infancy. HEADS IN THE SAND
"People who have ignored EMU have found to their cost that it has affected the markets," Deutsche Morgan Grenfell chief economist Steven Bell said.
"If EMU happens, it will be one of the most dramatic financial changes of this century."
For most bankers now, that idea is no longer an "if".
"It is only now that most people realise something is going to happen and they had better take their heads out of the sand and do something about it," a banker at a major U.S. house said.

Lehman Brothers managing director Philip Howard said the U.S. firm has set up a working group of a dozen people which he co-chairs. "Banks in Britain are a mixture of people who haven't woken up at all, to people who are taking EMU quite seriously."
Howard said one of the major impacts for banks would be systems changes, and Lehman is addressing this -- "So that we can process things on day one."
But many British and Japanese banks are still in the fledgling stages of EMU-strategy and feel flexibility to be key.

Those spoken to were vague about internal operational strategy and preferred to take the common line among British politicians, namely that decisions on EMU should be put off to the last moment because of multiple uncertainties.
One British bank EMU-spokesman was reluctant to talk about EMU, calling it "a sensitive topic inextricably linked to politics".

DMG's Bell said Continental Europe was more prepared. "They believe it is going to happen. In London, until very recently, people didn't believe it was going to happen...But now they do, and it's getting closer."
"We've put an enormous amount of work and effort into the EMU process, and it really affects us at all levels," he added.
EMU is due to start on January 1, 1999, with the creation of the European Central Bank (ECB) and the introduction of the euro single currency.
Current expectations are that it will initially include Austria, Belgium, Finland, France, Germany, Ireland, Luxembourg and the Netherlands.
Following are a few case studies of what some banks contacted by Reuters have done to prepare for EMU.
Deutsche Bank/Deutsche Morgan Grenfell is seen to have one of the more ambitious and transparent strategies.

Among other things it has made plans to centralise business in London and Frankfurt. Trading, pricing and origination will be centralised while sales will be decentralised in order to be closer to clients.

Bell said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell has required every head of staff to analyse the implications of EMU on their business and has produced a booklet on EMU for all staff, with the view that anyone from the chief economist to a retail bank tiller can answer customer questions on EMU.
Deutsche Bank will overhaul systems and procedures for the retail banking side and has set plans to offer clients accounts in euros from day one, he said.
It also expects more credit analysts and fewer macroeconomists as there will be less central bank watching.
A major U.S. investment bank said it had set up an "EMU taskforce" of 30 people in the past six months as part of a six-step process towards EMU.

The six steps are -- collecting information, formalising planning processes, establishing working groups, assessing the impact of the change-over, setting a defined strategy, calendar and budget, and establishing communication and training.
"As we progress, we'll have to get a project specialist to work full-time on this," the bank's EMU-team leader said.
The bank sees trading teams centralised and an increase in the number of sales staff spread out across Europe.
One large French bank has set up an internal EMU-steering committee of 10 people. Most of the group is made up of staff from the custody and securities department.
The bank participates in all the various EMU-working groups in France and London which try to tackle technical issues. It also has a special EMU research team.

It said it may relocate some traders from London to either Paris or Frankfurt, and it is working at preventing non-Continental London-based banks from running any active business in EMU bonds on the Continent. TWISTS AND TURNS AHEAD
But a cross-section of investment banks agree there is uncertainty about details, timing and customer-demand. They also fear the potentially large transition costs.
"It is a difficult climate in which to be very precise," an EMU-spokesman at a French bank said.
"The practical rules of convention concerning stocks, bonds and securities have not been made," another French banker said.
An economist at a U.S. bank added, "No one has a blueprint on EMU. There are still a lot of twists and turns ahead."
